works.name: Ho System
works.short_description: Published open methodology for human-AI collaborative software development in which the human practitioner maintains full architectural authority while using AI as an implementation partner. The core unit is a ho — a bounded ~2-hour session producing something real, connecting to the project arc via commit hash, ending with structured reflection. Practitioners progress through Shu-Ha-Ri stages; tiered understanding (Black Box, Functional, Deep) gives an honest frame for tracking what's understood versus delegated.
substantive_description: The dominant frame for AI-assisted development assumes the model leads. Vibe coding names the position with unembarrassed clarity: the human gestures, the model generates, the human accepts or rejects. The Ho System refuses the position.

It treats AI as an implementation partner inside a discipline the human owns — architectural authority held, structural decisions made consciously, every session bounded, every artifact reviewed. Eight production systems shipped under it, including a computer vision platform at Harvard and a ZFS backup orchestrator with 278 tests at 99% coverage.

The deeper claim is about agency in the age of capable models. Capable models tempt the practitioner to delegate the parts of the work that build the practitioner's judgment. The Ho System is the operational answer to that temptation: a methodology that lets you ship without becoming someone who cannot ship alone.

works.name: Dandori
works.hero: A prompt is a sentence; a handoff is an artifact.
works.short_description: Methodology for autonomous coding agent prep discipline. A prompt is a sentence; a handoff is an artifact. Dandori transforms planning conversations into bounded markdown specs that the agent reads as one unit of work. Published as a Skill on GitHub. Sits alongside the Ho System: where Ho structures the practitioner's session, Dandori structures the agent's brief.
substantive_description: The current generation of coding agents is capable of running unattended for hours on tasks they will get spectacularly wrong if briefed casually. The failure mode is structural: prompts are sentences, and sentences are the wrong artifact for autonomous work. Dandori is the answer in methodology form — a discipline for converting planning conversations into bounded, reviewable specifications the agent treats as one unit of work. The metaphor is correct: a Japanese workshop's dandori is the prep that makes the skilled labor possible.

The deeper argument is about authorship of agent work: who decided what gets built, and where in the artifact chain that decision is recorded. Without Dandori the answer is nobody, nowhere. With Dandori the answer is the practitioner, in the spec. That distinction is the difference between agent work that's auditable and agent work that's autopilot.

relationships.note: Where Ho structures the practitioner's session, Dandori structures the agent's brief.

works.name: Kanyō
works.tech_stack: Python, FastAPI, YOLOv8, React, Tailwind, Docker; NVIDIA, Intel, and CPU-only hardware profiles
works.short_description: Production computer vision pipeline for wildlife monitoring. Streams from YouTube (or any rtsp/http source), runs YOLOv8 bird detection with a debounced state machine to suppress false positives, records arrival/departure clips, sends Telegram notifications. Companion web viewer provides a public event archive with HKSV-style timeline, visit statistics, live stream embeds. Deployed at Harvard's Memorial Hall monitoring peregrine falcons, developed for Nobel laureate economist Claudia Goldin and Harvard FAS. Species-agnostic architecture. Built from zero development experience in six weeks using the Ho System. 114 passing tests.
substantive_description: Kanyō is the existence proof. The methodology question — can a practitioner with strong systems thinking but no formal engineering background ship production AI? — needed an answer that wasn't a position paper. Six weeks. 114 tests. Deployed at Harvard, monitoring peregrine falcons through an academic partnership with a Nobel laureate. The system is real, and it works.

Beyond the personal evidence, Kanyō makes a more interesting argument: the kind of work this is — domain-specific computer vision with research-grade requirements — has historically required either a specialist engineering team or compromise on quality. The Ho System collapses the dichotomy. The deployment context matters: a peregrine falcon is not a benchmark. Harvard FAS is not a test environment. The system runs in production for a researcher who needed it to work. That's the evidence the methodology needed.

relationships.note: Six weeks, 114 tests, deployed at Harvard — the methodology's first existence proof.

works.name: Hōzō
works.tech_stack: Python, syncoid, Wake-on-LAN, WebAuthn, bootstrap web UI
works.short_description: Wake-on-demand ZFS backup orchestrator. Pushes ZFS snapshots to a low-power remote backup node using syncoid over SSH, waking the node only when a backup run is scheduled or triggered. Runs entirely on the source machine — no agent needed on the remote. Bootstrap web UI with WebAuthn passkey auth provides job dashboard, run history, log viewer, break-glass DR restore. 278 tests, 99% coverage, zero lint or type errors. Built in approximately three hours using the Ho System.
substantive_description: Hōzō is the second proof, and the more interesting one. Kanyō took six weeks; Hōzō took three hours. The delta is not about the projects' relative complexity — it's about the practitioner's progression through Shu, Ha, and Ri. The same person who needed six weeks to ship Kanyō shipped Hōzō between dinner and bedtime, with higher test coverage and lower error rate.

The methodology's claim isn't you can ship one thing this way. The methodology's claim is you become someone who ships this way. Hōzō is the documented evidence. The 278 tests aren't decoration. The 99% coverage isn't decoration. They're the receipts a skeptical reader requires before believing that a non-engineer running a disciplined practice can produce work indistinguishable from senior engineering output.

relationships.note: The Shu-Ha-Ri progression made shippable: three hours, 278 tests, 99% coverage.
The Kanyō-to-Hōzō delta — six weeks to three hours — is the practitioner-progression evidence.

works.name: Kinhin
works.hero: The zazen of the system, not the workshop.
works.tech_stack: Python 3.12, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, HTMX, Docker Compose
works.short_description: Structured workbench application for Ho System practitioners. A place to define a project arc, sequence the hos within it, write structured devlogs, track progression through Shu-Ha-Ri stages, build a navigable learning trajectory over time. MVP deliberately excludes IDE integration, git interaction, and AI assistance — it is a record-keeping and reflection tool, not an execution environment. The second major Ho System pilot (after Kanyō), built using the methodology it implements.
substantive_description: A practice you can't see is a practice you can't improve. Kinhin makes Ho System practice visible to its own practitioner — the arc of a project, the rhythm of its hos, the structural rotation between modes, the visible movement through Shu, Ha, and Ri. The deliberate exclusion of execution capability is the design point: Kinhin is the zazen of the system, not the workshop.

The deeper argument is that mastery requires reflection, and reflection requires infrastructure — the same infrastructure that lets a martial artist watch tape of their own practice or a clinician keep a procedural log. The model has near-infinite memory of code patterns and zero memory of your learning trajectory. Kinhin restores the asymmetry the right way around.

relationships.note: The practitioner workbench: arcs, hos, devlogs, and Shu-Ha-Ri progression as software.
The second major Ho System pilot, after Kanyō — demonstrating the methodology's generalizability.

works.name: Satori — Internal Affairs
works.hero: Governance lives in architecture, not in the model.
works.tech_stack: Python, Pydantic, SvelteKit, TypeScript; four-package monorepo
works.personal_stake: Built for my teenage daughter, who lives with epilepsy from a TBI. She loves medical dramas and has spent enough time in hospitals to want to understand the medicine.
works.short_description: Interactive medical mystery simulator. Players make genuine diagnostic decisions under pressure — ordering tests, forming differential diagnoses, managing uncertainty — with death as a possible consequence of error. Built as a demonstration of AI governance. Four-package monorepo: Anamnesis (LLM case-generation pipeline at design-time), Satori (deterministic game engine running frozen cases with no runtime generation), an LLM client abstraction layer, and Internal Affairs (SvelteKit frontend). Cases are generated once and frozen as immutable JSON — gameplay is deterministic and auditable even though the cases themselves are AI-authored.
substantive_description: Version one was a single prompt: present a case, let the LLM improvise. That broke fast — facts invented, diagnoses changed mid-game, contradictions everywhere. Version two separates generation, execution, and narration into three layers. An LLM pipeline grounded in rigorous medical research generates cases from structured seeds; cases are validated against a JSON schema and frozen. A deterministic engine runs gameplay — actions, time, vitals, deterioration, outcomes. A final LLM layer adds narrative color at runtime, tightly bounded: it describes what happens, never decides what's medically true. Four boundaries enforce these separations: Freeze, Truth, Narration, Provider.

This is what AI in safety-sensitive domains has to do. The toy version is a medical game for one teenager. The general argument is for every regulated domain: healthcare, finance, law. Where you draw the boundaries between generation, execution, and narration determines what AI is allowed to do, what humans evaluate, and what factual integrity is preserved. Satori is the working demonstration. Its paired companion in this body of work is Glassroom — same architectural principle, inverse direction.

relationships.note: Same architectural principle, inverse direction: Satori protects downstream consumers from upstream AI generation; Glassroom surfaces institutional data structured to be obscure. Both built for the same daughter.

works.name: Glassroom
works.hero: The system's defense was opacity. I built the instrument that removed it.
works.personal_stake: Built for my daughter, whose rare neurological condition defies institutional understanding. The school system she was inside had a tool that produced data about her education while being structured to make that data illegible to a parent trying to advocate for a child the institution didn't know how to see.
works.short_description: Open-source research instrument that scrapes Google Classroom at the student level and aggregates assignment data into a unified dashboard, CSV export, and PDF downloader — without requiring any Google API credentials. Playwright browser automation operates entirely within a student account, surfacing implementation variance between teachers that Google's own interface deliberately obscures: assignment counts, due-date usage, completion rates, structural patterns across all classes at once. Built originally for IEP advocacy. Harvard GSE research collaboration in pursuit for a multi-site empirical audit.
substantive_description: Assignments scattered across teachers, no aggregate view, no way to compare implementation between classrooms, no way to demonstrate the variance that was visibly affecting her. The system's defense was opacity. I built the instrument that removed it.

The architectural argument generalizes. Glassroom is the inverse companion to Satori: where Satori uses architecture to protect downstream consumers from upstream AI generation, Glassroom uses architecture to surface downstream institutional data that an upstream system was structured to obscure. Same principle of layer separation, deployed for inverse purposes. The pair makes the structural point: governance lives in the architecture, not in the model.

Both tools were built for the same daughter — different needs, same person being failed by existing options, same generalizable architectural argument extracted from a specific case of love and necessity. The pair is the work.

works.name: m4Bookmaker
works.hero: You own what you can hold, file by file, on your own machine.
works.short_description: Converts folders of MP3 (or other audio) files into clean, properly-chaptered M4B audiobooks for personal use. Ships as a signed macOS app and Windows installer; also distributed as a PyPI package. Full pipeline: automatic chapter detection from filenames, interactive visual chapter editor with built-in audio player, batch queue processing, automatic audio repair for common encoding problems. One of the first tools built under the Ho System; the GUI-to-CLI symmetry was a deliberate architectural choice to keep it scriptable without sacrificing approachability.
substantive_description: A small app with a large argument. m4Bookmaker exists because Audible's ecosystem treats audiobook ownership as a license rather than a possession — a contract that can be revoked, a format that won't move, a library that lives on someone else's server and at someone else's discretion. The technical solution is small (rebuild the M4B yourself from MP3s) and the philosophical position is large (you own what you can hold, file by file, on your own machine).

The deeper argument is digital sovereignty as a default rather than a niche concern. The Ho System made it shippable as a small project — concept to signed, packaged, distributed product in 3.5 days — but the position it embodies is structural. Every time a tool gets repossessed by its platform, a small piece of personal capacity dies. m4Bookmaker is the refusal of that pattern, sized to one specific failure.

relationships.note: One of the first Ho System builds: concept to signed, packaged, distributed product in 3.5 days.

works.name: Pink Teaming
works.hero: The cooperative counterpart to red teaming.
works.short_description: The Pink Teaming manifesto. The cooperative counterpart to red teaming — where red teaming probes models adversarially for failure modes, pink teaming reads them with sustained hermeneutic attention to develop the practitioner's judgment. Companion to the Destructive Interference white paper. Site live; argument published.
substantive_description: Most safety work on AI is adversarial or theoretical. Red teaming probes a single session for vulnerabilities. Theoretical safety reasons about ideal cases. Both miss the structural feature of how AI actually causes harm: the gradient of drift, sycophancy, and judgment erosion that compounds over months of sustained collaboration and is invisible in any one session. Pink Teaming is the missing layer — practitioner-side safety discipline that reads the model with sustained hermeneutic attention over time, surfacing the patterns that only emerge across extended use.

The deeper argument is about what safety thinking includes. Adversarial probing is necessary and insufficient. The practitioner — the person actually shipping AI-assisted work day after day — is operating in a different threat environment than the red team, and the discipline they need is structurally different. Pink Teaming names that discipline, models it, and argues that no AI safety program is complete without it.

relationships.note: Companion to the DI white paper; the two share the safety/diagnostic foundation.

works.name: Destructive Interference
works.hero: The degradation is structural, not lexical.
works.short_description: A diagnostic taxonomy of eight named structural failure classes in AI-influenced writing: Pre-emptive Evaluation, Performed Urgency, Throat-Clear, Balanced Hedge, Significance Stamp, Mirror Summary, Emotional Instruction, Manufactured Transition. Each has a defined mechanism, a diagnostic test, and documented examples drawn from corpus analysis. The intellectual foundation of the whole Constructive Interference program. White paper near publication, not yet published. Operationalized via Kiku; deployed as a generative constraint in the atm-correspondence skill.
substantive_description: The dominant conversation about AI writing degradation stops at vocabulary — the word "delve," the em-dash. The vocabulary frame is wrong. The degradation is structural. Destructive Interference is the taxonomy that names what's actually happening: eight specific rhetorical and structural failure modes that survive vocabulary substitution because they're not about which words appear but about how arguments are made, evidence is staged, and the reader is positioned. Each pattern reads as good writing until you have the taxonomy, after which you can't unsee them.

The deeper argument: most prose now is collaborative prose, whether the writer acknowledges the collaboration or not. The question isn't whether AI is involved in writing — that ship has sailed — but whether the writer has the diagnostic apparatus to detect where the collaboration has degraded the work. Destructive Interference is that apparatus. The white paper formalizes the framework academically; the craft essay companion demonstrates the failures and the corrections in worked examples. The pair argues that practitioner-side quality discipline is a real subfield and Destructive Interference is its founding taxonomy.

works.name: Kiku
works.hero: A taxonomy without instrumentation is a position paper.
works.tech_stack: Python (mypy strict, flake8, full test coverage), regex + Claude API; YAML-defined profiles
works.short_description: Hybrid regex + LLM extraction tool that processes AI conversation exports and surfaces patterns of language behavior. YAML-defined profiles enable two-tier detection: fast regex matching in Tier 1 for literal patterns, Claude API semantic classification in Tier 2 for patterns that resist rules. Built to operationalize the Destructive Interference taxonomy — the diagnostic framework needed an instrument that could scale. In active personal use; built to the full Ho verification stack.
substantive_description: A diagnostic framework that can't scale to corpus is a diagnostic framework that can't generalize. Kiku is the operational answer — a two-tier detector that runs the DI taxonomy across the practitioner's accumulated AI conversation history at speed. The deeper argument is methodological: a taxonomy without instrumentation is a position paper. Instrumentation without a taxonomy is automated nothing. Kiku closes the loop. It makes the eight named failure classes actionable at corpus scale, which is the only scale at which sustained AI collaboration actually happens.

relationships.note: Two-tier detection: regex for literal patterns, Claude API semantic classification for patterns that resist rules.

works.name: *, Actually
works.hero: Enter with a question, navigate by relationship, stop when you understand enough.
works.short_description: Domain-agnostic system for making relational technical knowledge navigable: enter with a question, navigate by concept relationship, stop when you understand enough. Progressive-disclosure design — every concept has depth layers (name, definition, usage, relationships, full theory) and the reader controls how far they go rather than being forced through a linear document. Organized around mental models and questions, not product features or chapters. SSH, Actually is the first complete content set. Replicable across any field where understanding concept relationships matters more than memorizing isolated facts.
substantive_description: Most technical documentation is written by the people who built the thing for the people who already understand the field. The result is reference material that fails the actual job of getting someone from I have a question to I understand enough to act. *, Actually is the answer in methodology form: organize knowledge by question and relationship rather than by product surface. Let the reader dial the depth they need. Make the mental models explicit before the commands. Be honest about where the subject is confusing.

The deeper argument is about the relationship between knowledge architecture and reader agency. The reader of a typical man page has no agency — the content was structured for an internal logic that has nothing to do with what the reader wants to know. *, Actually is what reader agency looks like when the architecture is built to support it.

works.name: SSH, Actually
works.short_description: First content set in the *, Actually knowledge architecture system. Comprehensive guide to SSH, key pairs, hardware security keys, and modern authentication using a definition-first approach: mental models before commands, honest about where the subject is confusing, organized around concept relationships rather than product features. Covers SSH fundamentals, cryptographic primitives, FIDO2, passkeys, hardware security keys, with a companion commands reference. HTMX-based, terminal-aesthetic, keyboard-driven, zero framework overhead.
substantive_description: A specific demonstration of *, Actually inside a specific domain whose existing documentation is famously bad. SSH is a system every working developer needs, every working developer pretends to understand, and almost no one was taught well. The official documentation describes commands; the field needs mental models. SSH, Actually starts where understanding starts and works outward through relationships.

The deeper argument is that the same approach generalizes. Any technical domain whose documentation has accumulated as features-of-tools rather than relationships-between-concepts has the same opportunity. SSH, Actually is the first instance of the answer.

relationships.note: The first complete content set demonstrating the *, Actually system.
